3.39.m:
Nārada said: / Then, having reached Sandhyā and Savidyā, an excellent holy bath,
and sipping water, a man becomes learned; of this there is no doubt.

By the grace of Rāma, the king of holy baths was created anciently;
reaching that Lauhitya, he would obtain much gold.

Reaching the Karatoyā and fasting for three nights, a man
obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to Indra's realm.

Moreover, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, O king of kings,
the wise declare [the fruit is] ten times that of a horse sacrifice.

Whoever reaches the further island of the Gaṅgā and bathes, O Bhārata,
fasting for three nights, O king, will obtain every desire.

Then, going to the Vaitaraṇī, the river that liberates from sin,
and reaching the Viraja holy bath, he shines like the moon.

Purifying his family by its power, he removes every sin;
having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows, the man purifies his own family.

Dwelling pure at the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotirathā,
having gratified the ancestors and the gods, he obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

At the source of the Śoṇa and the Narmadā, O best of Kurus,
having sipped water at Vaṃśagulma, he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

Reaching the Ṛṣabha holy bath in Kośalā, O ruler of men,
a man who fasts for three nights obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice.

Reaching Kośalā, one should sip water at the Kāla holy bath;
he receives eleven times [the fruit of the gift of] a bull; there is no doubt about this.

Sipping water at the Puṣpavatī, a man who fasts for three nights
would find the fruit of a thousand cows and elevate his lineage.

Then, having bathed at the Badārikā holy bath with a restrained mind,
he attains a long life and goes to the heavenly realm.

Then, reaching Mahendra, frequented by the son of Jamadagni,
a man who bathes in Rāmatīrtha obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

Mataṅga's Kedāra is also right there, O bull of the Bharatas;
having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Approaching Śrīparvata, one should touch the water of the riverbank;
he obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.

On Śrīparvata, the great god Mahādeva of great splendor,
exceedingly pleased, dwelt together with the Goddess, and Brahmā surrounded by the gods.

Bathing there in Devahrada, pure and with a restrained mind,
he obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.

Going to Mount Ṛṣabha, revered by the gods among the Bhāṇḍas,
he obtains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya sacrifice and rejoices upon the surface of heaven.

Then one should go to the Kāverī, surrounded by troops of apsarases;
having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

At that holy bath of the ocean, one should sip water at Kanyātīrtha;
having sipped water there, O king of kings, one is freed from all sins.

Then, having reached Gokarṇa, renowned in the three worlds,
in the midst of the ocean, O king of kings, bowed to by all worlds,

where gods headed by Brahmā, sages rich in asceticism,
spirits, yakṣas, piśācas, and kinnaras along with great serpents,

siddhas, cāraṇas, gandharvas, human beings, and snakes,
rivers, oceans, and mountains worship the husband of Umā,

worshiping Īśāna there, a man who fasts for three nights
obtains [the fruit of] ten horse sacrifices and acquires leadership of the Gaṇas.

Fasting for twelve nights, a man achieves his aim.
Right there is the abode of Gāyatrī, renowned in the three worlds.

Staying there for three nights, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows;
and there is an ocular proof for brāhmaṇas, O ruler of men:

If a twice-born born of miscegenation recites the Gāyatrī,
his speech turns into a secular verse or a song, O king.

When a non-brāhmaṇa recites it, the Sāvitrī is destroyed.
Having reached the hard-to-attain pool of the brāhmaṇa sage Saṃvarta,

one becomes endowed with beauty and is born fortunate.
Then, having reached the Veṇā, one should gratify the ancestors and gods;

a man obtains an aerial chariot joined with peacocks and swans.
Then, reaching the Godāvarī, ever frequented by the perfected ones,

he obtains [the fruit of] a Gavāmayana sacrifice and goes to the realm of Vāyu.
Bathing at the confluence of the Veṇā, he obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

Bathing at the confluence of the Varadā, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Reaching Brahmasthūṇā, a man who fasts for three nights

would find the fruit of a thousand cows and go to the heavenly realm.
Reaching Kubjāvana, chaste and composed,

fasting for three nights and bathing, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Then, bathing in Devahrada, at the source of the Kṛṣṇaveṇā's waters,

and at the Jyotirmātra pool, and likewise at Kanyāśrama, O king,
where, having sacrificed with a hundred rites, the king of the gods went to heaven,

he would find [the fruit of] a hundred Agniṣṭomas merely by going there.
Bathing in the pool of all gods, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Bathing in the Jātimātra pool, a man will remember his past lives.
Going to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and of the great-souled Śuka,

devoted to worshiping the ancestors and the gods, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Reaching the Daṇḍaka forest, O great king, one should sip water.

Going to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and of the great-souled Śuka,
a man does not meet an evil destiny and purifies his family.

Then one should go to Sūryāraka, frequented by Jamadagni;
bathing in Rāmatīrtha, a man would obtain much gold.

Bathing in Saptagodāvarī, self-controlled and eating restricted food,
he attains great merit and goes to the realm of the gods.

Then one should go to Devapatha, self-controlled and eating restricted food;
whatever merit belongs to a divine sacrifice, that a human being obtains.

Reaching the Tuṅgaka forest, chaste and with senses restrained,
[where] in ancient times Sārasvata taught the Vedas to the sages.

There, the son of the sage Āṅgirasa, seated upon the upper garments
of the great sages, when the Vedas were lost, O Bhārata,

with the [oṃ]kāra properly uttered according to rule—
whatever had been studied by someone before presented itself to him.

The sages were there, and the gods, Varuṇa, Agni, Prajāpati,
Hari, the god Nārāyaṇa, and Mahādeva likewise,

and the divine Grandfather of great splendor, along with the gods,
appointed the intensely radiant Bhṛgu for the purpose of performing the sacrifice.
Then that lord, following the rule, performed for all the sages / the re-establishment [of their sacred fires] through the rite seen by the gods.
Gratified there properly with their share of clarified butter, / the gods went to the three worlds, and the sages as they pleased.
Of one who enters that forest, Tuṅgaka, O best of kings, / the sin of a woman or a man is immediately destroyed.
A wise man should dwell there for a month, restrained and eating measured food; / he goes to the world of Brahmā, O king, and purifies his family again.
Reaching Medhāvana, one should satisfy the ancestors and gods; / he attains the Agniṣṭoma and acquires memory and intelligence.
Going there to Kālañjara, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows; / O king, one should cultivate the self there on Mount Kālañjara.
A man is honored in the heavenly world; of this there is no doubt. / Then, O lord of the people, at Citrakūṭa, the foremost of excellent mountains,
having reached the Mandākinī, the river that frees one from sin, / performing ablutions there and devoted to worshipping the ancestors and gods,
one obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the supreme destination. / Then, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed place of Guha,
where the god Mahāsena is eternally present, O king; / by merely going there, a man attains perfection, O best of men.
Bathing at Koṭitīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows; / having circumambulated, a man goes to the abode of fame.
Having approached Mahādeva, he shines like the moon. / There is a well there, O great king, renowned, O bull of the Bharatas,
in which the four oceans reside, O Yudhiṣṭhira. / Having sipped water there, O king of kings, and having circumambulated,
a self-restrained man, purified, goes to the supreme destination. / Then, O best of the Kurus, one should go to great Śṛṅgaverapura,
where previously the very wise Rāma, son of Daśaratha, crossed [the Gaṅgā]. / Bathing in the Gaṅgā, a celibate student with senses conquered,
having shaken off his sins, becomes pure and obtains [the fruit of] the Vājapeya. / Then one should go to Muñjavaṭa, the abode of the wise god [Śiva].
Having approached and worshipped Mahādeva, O ruler of men, / and having circumambulated, one attains the state of a leader of [Śiva’s] hosts.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to Prayāga, praised by the sages, / where the gods headed by Brahmā, the quarters, and the lords of the quarters,
the guardians of the worlds, the Siddhas, the devoted ancestors, / and the great sages headed by Sanatkumāra [reside],
as well as the Nāgas, the Suparṇas, the Siddhas holding brilliance, / the rivers and the oceans, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
and the divine Hari is present there, honored by Prajāpati. / There are three pools there, and between them flows the Jāhnavī;
passing through Prayāga, she is honored above all holy places. / There the daughter of the sun, renowned in the three worlds,
the Yamunā, joins with the Gaṅgā, blessing the world. / Between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is remembered as the hips of the earth;
the sages know Prayāga as the end of the hips, the generative organ. / Prayāga, Supratiṣṭhāna, both Kambala and Aśvatara,
and the holy place Bhogavatī are declared as the altar of Prajāpati. / There the Vedas and the sacrifices, embodied, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
and the great, sinless sages attend upon Prajāpati; / they worship the gods with sacrifices, and likewise the wielder of the discus, O king.
Therefore, there is nothing more holy in the three worlds, O descendant of Bharata; / Prayāga surpasses all holy places in its power, O lord.
From hearing of that holy place, from even chanting its name, / or from bowing one's head [to it], one is freed from all sins.
One who takes a bath at that confluence, firm in vows, / attains the very great merit of the Rājasūya and the horse sacrifice.
For this is the sacrificial ground even of the gods; so it is told. / Even a very small gift given there becomes great, O descendant of Bharata.
Neither by the word of a god, dear one, nor by the word of the people / should your mind be turned away concerning dying at Prayāga.
Ten thousand holy places and another sixty crores [of them], / whose presence is proclaimed right here, O joy of the Kurus.
Whatever merit lies in the four Vedas, and whatever in those who speak the truth, / one who merely bathes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā obtains that.
Then there is the excellent holy place named Bhogavatī, belonging to Vāsuki; / one who takes a bath there would obtain [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice.
There is the holy place Haṃsaprapatana, renowned in the three worlds, / and Daśāśvamedhika upon the Gaṅgā, O joy of the Kurus.
The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever it is plunged into, / especially at Kanakhala, while Prayāga is supreme and great.
Even if one who has committed a hundred misdeeds serves the Gaṅgā, / the water of the Gaṅgā burns all of it away, as fire burns fuel.
The water of the Gaṅgā burns all, like fire burns a heap of cotton. / Puṣkara is remembered as holy in all the Kṛta age, and in Tretā;
in Dvāpara it is Kurukṣetra, and the Gaṅgā is remembered in the Kali yuga. / At Puṣkara one should practice austerity; at Mahālaya one should give gifts;
at Malaya one should enter fire; at Bhṛgutuṅga [one should undertake] fasting. / At Puṣkara, at Kurukṣetra, and among those who enter the waters of the Gaṅgā,
a creature instantly redeems seven ancestors and seven descendants. / Praised, she purifies sin; seen, she grants merit.
Plunged into and drunk, she purifies the family up to the seventh generation. / As long as a man's bone touches the water of the Gaṅgā,
for that long, O king, that person is honored in the heavenly world. / Just as holy places and holy shrines,
once attended upon and merit gained, make one share in the other world, / [so] there is no holy place like the Gaṅgā, no deity higher than Keśava,
and nothing higher than the Brahmins; thus spoke the grandfather [Brahmā]. / Wherever the Gaṅgā is, O great king, that region extends for a yojana,
and it should be known as a Siddha field, resting upon the bank of the Gaṅgā. / This is the truth in the minds of twice-born men and good people,
and one should whisper liberation into the ear of a disciplined and faithful disciple. / This is lawful, this is pure, this leads to heaven, this brings happiness;
this is most holy, charming, purifying, the highest dharma, / this secret crown of the earth, delivering from all sins.
Reciting it in the midst of the twice-born, one attains purity; / it is auspicious, heaven-bestowing, greatly meritorious, quelling rivals, benevolent.
The recitation of the succession of holy places is the foremost source of wisdom: / the childless obtains a son, the poor attains wealth,
a king conquers the earth, a Vaiśya obtains wealth, / a Śūdra attains his desired wishes, and a Brahmin, reading it, crosses over to the far shore.
And he who constantly hears this, ever pure with the merit of the holy places, / attains recollection of past births and rejoices on the summit of heaven.
The holy places described are accessible, and some are inaccessible; / one may also approach them mentally with devotion to all holy places.
These were made by the Vasus, Sādhyas, Ādityas, Maruts, and Aśvins, / and by sages like gods, who sought meritorious deeds.
Thus you too, O descendant of Kuru, steadfast in vows, according to this rule, / go to the holy places with self-restraint; merit increases through merit.
By means of senses previously purified, out of faith and insight into the scriptures, / these holy places are reached by the virtuous who follow the righteous.
Not one who has failed to act, nor one whose self is uncultivated, nor an impure person, nor a thief / bathes in the sacred fords, O descendant of Kuru, nor does a deceitful man.

By you, however, of upright conduct, who ever discern duty and purpose, / all the fathers, dear one, and great-grandfathers have been gratified with libations, / as have the gods headed by the grandfathers, along with the hosts of seers.
Vasiṣṭha said: And you, O knower of dharma, have by your righteousness ever delighted them; / O Dilīpa, you will attain great and eternal fame on earth.
Nārada said: Having spoken thus and taken his leave, the blessed seer Vasiṣṭha, / pleased in his heart, vanished right there.
Dilīpa, O tiger among the Kurus, through seeing the true purpose of the scriptures / and on Vasiṣṭha's word, traversed the earth.
Thus, O fortunate one, this highly sacred pilgrimage to fords, / freeing from all sins, has been established at Pratiṣṭhāna.
Whoever wanders the earth according to this rule / shall, having departed, enjoy the full fruit of a hundred horse sacrifices.
And after that, O son of Pṛthā, you will attain supreme righteousness eightfold, / just as King Dilīpa, O son of Pṛthā, previously attained it.
Because you guide the seers, your reward will be eightfold; / for these sacred fords, O descendant of Bharata, are overrun by hosts of demons.
There is no recourse for anyone else apart from you, O joy of the Kurus. / This deed of the divine seer pertains to all the sacred fords.
Whoever rising early recites it is freed from all sins, / where the foremost seers are ever present: Vālmīki, then Kaśyapa,
and Ātreya, then Kauṇḍinya, Viśvāmitra, then Gautama, / Asita, and Devala, and Mārkaṇḍeya, then Gālava,
and the disciple of Bharadvāja, the sage Uddālaka, / Śaunaka together with his son, and Vyāsa, the foremost of ascetics,
and Durvāsas, best of sages, and Jābāli of great austerities. / All these excellent seers, rich in austerities, await you.
Together with them, O fortunate one, visit these sacred fords; / you will attain great fame just like King Mahābhiṣa.
As righteous Yayāti, and as King Purūravas, / so you, O tiger among the Kurus, shine through your own righteousness.
As King Bhagīratha, and as celebrated Rāma, / and as indeed the slayer of Vṛtra consumed all his rivals in ancient times,
and the king of gods protected the three worlds free from anxiety, / so, having destroyed your enemies, you will protect the subjects.
Having obtained the earth won through your own righteousness, O lotus-eyed one, / you will attain renown through prowess, like Kārttavīrya Arjuna.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to the king, the blessed seer Nārada, / taking leave of the great king, vanished right there.
Righteous Yudhiṣṭhira also, true to his vows, the lord of the earth, / with deep reverence went to all the sacred fords together with the seers.
O all you seers, this narrative regarding the pilgrimage to fords has been told by me; / whoever recites or hears it is freed from all sins.
All the essential truth has been told by me; what more do you wish to hear? / Indeed, of the seers of holy renown, there is nothing that I should not say.

3.40.m: Sūta said: Thus the sacred fords have been spoken of, bodies of Viṣṇu, O you of noble vows; / from contact with any one of these, a man becomes liberated.
Blessed is the hearing of sacred fords, blessed is the resort to sacred fords; / there is no other means for the destruction of the mass of sins in the Kali age.
"May I dwell at a sacred ford; likewise may I touch a sacred ford"— / whoever speaks thus daily goes to the highest, supreme [state].
His sins are destroyed merely by conversing about sacred fords; / sacred fords are indeed blessed, to be attended by the blessed, O you of noble vows.
By the very attendance on sacred fords the Lord is attended, / Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the world; there is no abode higher than a sacred ford.
A Brāhmaṇa, the tulasī, the aśvattha tree, an assemblage of sacred fords, / and Viṣṇu, the supreme Lord—these should ever be served by men.
Especially the service of Brāhmaṇas, O bull-like sages, / the first-born know to be greater than bathing in all sacred fords and the like.
Therefore, a wise person should daily worship the foot of a twice-born, which is auspicious and embodies all sacred fords; / that would be greater than a sacred ford.
One should circumambulate the aśvattha tree, the tulasī, and cows; / having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords, one is exalted in the world of Viṣṇu.
Therefore one should destroy evil actions through the resort to sacred fords; / otherwise one goes to hell, for [sin] is pacified through the experiencing of karma.
The residence of sinners is in hell; the virtuous one enjoys heaven; / therefore, a discerning person should certainly resort to a sacred ford, which is merit.
The seers said: Indeed, the sacred fords have been heard together with their glorifications, O you of noble vows; / now we wish to hear the particulars of Prayāga.
Prayāga was spoken of in brief by you formerly, O Sūta; / we wish to hear of it in detail; let it be told to us, O Sūta!
Sūta said: Well asked, O fortunate ones, of noble vows, concerning Prayāga; / well then, I will declare the detailed description of Prayāga,
which was recounted formerly by Mārkaṇḍeya to the son of Pāṇḍu, / when the Bhārata [war] had taken place and the son of Pṛthā had obtained the kingdom.
In the meantime, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, / tormented by grief for his kinsmen, kept thinking again and again:
"King Duryodhana was the lord of eleven armies; / having tormented us exceedingly, all of them have gone to destruction.
Relying on Vāsudeva, only five Pāṇḍavas remain. / How [did we slay] Droṇa, and Bhīṣma, and Karṇa of mighty strength,
and King Duryodhana together with his brothers and sons? / All the kings have been slain, and whoever else considered themselves heroes.
Bereft of kingdom, what should be done? What with pleasures or with life? / Woe! Alas!"—thinking thus, the king was overwhelmed with despair.
Motionless, without enthusiasm, he stood for a while with downcast face. / When the king regained his senses, he kept pondering again and again:
"What practice, observance, or sacred ford should I follow by rule, / by which I might quickly be liberated from the defilement of great sins,
where a man, having bathed, goes to the unexcelled world of Viṣṇu? / Indeed, how can I ask Kṛṣṇa, by whom this great deed was caused to be done?
How can I ask Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose hundred sons have been slain? / How can I ask Vyāsa, whose family has been destroyed?"
Thus Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was reduced to despondency; / all the Pāṇḍavas wept, overwhelmed with grief for their kinsmen,
as did the great-souled ones gathered there who depended on the Pāṇḍavas, / and Kuntī and Draupadī, and whoever had arrived there.
All fell to the earth, weeping all around. / In Vārāṇasī, however, Yudhiṣṭhira was perceived by Mārkaṇḍa,
how he was reduced to despondency, weeping and deeply sorrowful. / In a very short time, Mārkaṇḍa of great austerities
arrived at Hastināpura and stood at the royal gate. / The doorkeeper, seeing him, spoke quickly to the king:
"The sage Mārkaṇḍa, wishing to see you, stands at the gate." / Then the son of Dharma, eager, approached the gate quickly.

Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Welcome to you, O greatly wise one! Welcome to you, O great sage!
Today my birth has borne fruit; today my family is purified.

Today my ancestors are satisfied, now that you have been seen, O great sage!
Having placed him upon a throne, with washing of the feet, worship, and the like,

the great-souled Yudhiṣṭhira indeed worshipped that sage.
Then Mārkaṇḍa said to him: "I have been honored by you, O lord.

Speak swiftly, O king, why was [this done] in haste by you?
Or by what have you become distressed? Tell it before me."

Yudhiṣṭhira said:
And what happened to us for the sake of the kingdom, O great sage—
knowing all this indeed, the venerable one has come here.

how much less so through the duty of kings, especially for a kṣatriya!
Therefore, keeping this in your heart, one should not worry about sin.

Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having bowed his head to the sage, [said:]
"I ask you, O best of sages, who always see the three times:
tell me concisely, whereby I may be freed from sin."

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O fortunate king, to what you ask me, O descendant of Bharata:
thus Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and also the holy ford, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

How much more [merit] was indeed praised of old by meritorious brāhmaṇas, O lord!
Going to Prayāga is the best for men of virtuous deeds.

3.41.m:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O venerable one, I wish to hear how it stood in an earlier cosmic age,
and how is the journey to Prayāga, of what nature for men there?

What is the destination of those who die there, and what is the fruit for those who have bathed?
And what is the fruit for those who reside at Prayāga? Tell [me].
Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is great indeed.

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall tell you, my child, whatever fruit is desired by the lord,
which was heard by me of old being spoken by the ṛṣis and vipras.

From Prayāga up to Pratiṣṭhāna, from the Dharmakī pool to Vāsuki's pool,
the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, and the Bahumūlika Nāgas—

this field of Prajāpati is celebrated in the three worlds.
Having bathed here, they go to heaven; those who have died are free from rebirth.

There the gods, headed by Brahmā, assemble and keep guard.
And there are many other holy fords that destroy all sins,

which cannot be spoken of, O king, even in many hundreds of years.
I shall proclaim concisely the celebration of Prayāga.

Sixty thousand bows protect the Jāhnavī.
Savitar, drawn by seven steeds, always protects the Yamunā.

Vāsava himself especially protects Prayāga.
Hari, along with the gods, protects the circle agreed upon.

The trident-bearing Maheśvara constantly protects that banyan tree.
The god indeed protects the auspicious place that removes all sins.

A person enveloped in adharma never goes to that abode.
When his sin has become slight or very small, O ruler of men,

for one remembering Prayāga, everything comes to destruction.
Even by the sight of that holy ford, or by reciting its name,

or by obtaining its clay, a man is freed from sin.
There are five pools, O king of kings, in the midst of which is the Jāhnavī.

For one who has entered Prayāga, sin dissolves that very moment.
The man who remembers the Gaṅgā across thousands of yojanas,

even if he has committed evil deeds, attains the supreme destination.
By praising [her] he is freed from sins; having seen [her] he sees good fortune;

having bathed and having drunk, he purifies his family up to the seventh [generation].
Speaking the truth, having conquered anger, fully dedicated to non-violence,

following dharma, knowing reality, devoted to the welfare of cows and brāhmaṇas,
bathed between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, one is freed from sin.

He fully obtains his desired wishes in abundance, conceived in mind.
Then, having gone to Prayāga, which is protected by all the gods,

living as a celibate student for a month, he should offer libations to ancestors and gods;
he obtains desired wishes wherever he is born.

Where the goddess, the daughter of Tapana, renowned in the three worlds,
the fortunate river Yamunā, joins [the Gaṅgā],

there the god Maheśvara is always directly present.
Virtue at Prayāga is hard to attain for human beings, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas,
having touched water there, O king of kings, are glorified in the heavenly world.

3.42.m:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen again, O king, to the glorification of Prayāga,
having gone to which one is freed from all sins, there is no doubt in this.

For the afflicted, the poor, and those of firm resolve,
setting aside the place Prayāga, there is never anything imperishable.

The one who, having reached the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, abandons his life,
in an aerial chariot shining with the color of gold, with the radiance of the sun,

in the midst of gandharvas and apsarases, that human being rejoices in heaven;
he attains his desired wishes—so the best of ṛṣis say.

With divine [chariots] made of all gems, crowded with various flags,
and filled with excellent women of auspicious signs, he rejoices.

Asleep, he is awakened by the sounds of song and musical instruments;
as long as he does not remember [another] birth, so long is he honored in heaven.

Falling from that heaven, with his karma exhausted, fallen from the sky,
he is born in a prosperous family filled with gold and jewels.

He remembers that very holy ford; from remembering, he goes there.
Whether situated in the countryside or in a forest, in a foreign land or at home,

even by merely remembering Prayāga, he who abandons his life
attains the world of Brahmā—so the best of ṛṣis say.

Where the golden earth is filled with all desired fruits,
where ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas go in that world,

on the auspicious, charming bank of the Mandākinī crowded with thousands of women,
he rejoices together with the ṛṣis through his deed performed here.

He is worshipped in heaven by siddhas, cāraṇas, gandharvas, and deities;
then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes the lord of Jambudvīpa.

Then, constantly meditating upon auspicious deeds,
he becomes virtuous and endowed with wealth in this world, there is no doubt.

Established in truth and dharma by action, mind, and speech,
he who gives a gift between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,

whether gold, gems, pearls, or grain, [or receives] an acceptance of a gift,
for his own sake, for ancestral rites, or even in worship of the deities,

that holy ford becomes fruitless for him so long as he consumes that fruit.
Thus one should not accept [gifts] at a holy ford or at sacred sanctuaries.

And on all occasions, a twice-born should be vigilant.
He who gives a tawny, reddish-brown cow at Prayāga,

with golden horns, silver hooves, a cloth around its neck, and full of milk,
having caused a virtuous, learned Vedic scholar to receive it according to rule at Prayāga—

one wearing white garments, peaceful, knowing dharma, and master of the Veda—
that cow should be given to him at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,

along with costly garments and various gems,
for as many hairs as there are on the limbs of that cow, O best of men.
For as many thousands of years he is exalted in the world of heaven; / wherever he takes birth, that cow is born there too.
And through that deed he never sees terrible hell; / having reached the Northern Kurus, he rejoices for imperishable time.
From hundreds of thousands of cows one should give one milch cow; / a single cow rescues sons, wives, and servants.
Therefore, of all gifts the gift of a cow is superior; / in difficult, uneven, terrible situations, when great sins arise, / the cow provides protection; therefore it should be given to a twice-born.

3.43.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / In the manner the glorification of Prayāga has been narrated by you, O sage, / in that very manner I am freed from all sins, there is no doubt.
O Lord, by what rule should those of resolute dharma proceed? / Tell me, O great sage, the rule that is proclaimed for Prayāga.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / I will narrate to you, child, the orderly rule of pilgrimage to holy places, / for one who would go, O best of the Kurus, to Prayāga accompanied by gods.
Mounted on an ox—hear also the fruit of that [deed]: / he dwells in a terrible hell, in the most dreadful wrath of cows.
And the ancestors of that embodied soul do not accept water. / But whoever bathes and gives drink to children and young ones,
just as to himself, so to all, and causes gifts to be given to Brāhmaṇas— / whatever man, out of longing for power or out of delusion, goes by vehicle,
for him that holy place is fruitless; therefore one should abandon a vehicle. / But whoever gives away a maiden between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā,
according to the rule of the sages, to the best of his wealth, / he does not see terrible Yama or hell through that deed.
Having gone to the Northern Kurus, he rejoices for imperishable time; / and he obtains sons and wives who are righteous and endowed with wisdom.
Gifts should be given there according to one's wealth; / through that, by the fruit of the holy place itself, it increases, there is no doubt.
He remains in heaven, O king of kings, until the dissolution of beings. / Whoever abandons his life taking refuge at the root of the banyan tree,
having passed beyond all worlds, goes to the world of Rudra. / There the twelve suns blaze, resting upon Rudra;
they burn up the entire universe, but the root of the banyan tree is not burned. / And when the universe has become a single ocean, with moon, sun, and wind destroyed,
Viṣṇu sleeps right here, being born again and again. / Gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas
always frequent that holy place at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. / They go there, O king of kings, and that which is united at Prayāga—
there are Brahmā and the other gods, the directions and the lords of the directions, / the world-guardians, the Sādhyas, and the ancestors respected by the world,
the supreme sages headed by Sanatkumāra, / and the other sage-seers headed by Aṅgiras,
and the Nāgas, the Siddhas, the Suparṇas, and those who move in the sky, / the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, the Nāgas, and the Vidyādharas.
And Lord Hari sits there, placed at the head by Prajāpati. / Between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is considered the hips of the earth.
Prayāga, O tiger among kings, is famed in the three worlds; / there is nothing more meritorious than it in the three worlds, O Bhārata.
By hearing about that holy place, or even by reciting its name, / or even by touching its soil, a person is freed from sin.
Whoever, having strict vows, performs bathing at that confluence / obtains a fruit equal to the Rājasūya and the horse sacrifice.
Neither by the word of the Veda, dear one, nor by the word of ordinary people / should your mind be turned away from going to Prayāga.
Ten thousand holy places and another sixty crores— / their presence is right here by recital [of it], O delight of the Kurus.
The destination of a wise sage who is engaged in yoga and upright / is the destination of one who relinquishes life at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
They live in vain in this world wherever they are, O Yudhiṣṭhira, / who have not reached Prayāga, famed in the three worlds.
Having thus seen that holy place Prayāga, the supreme state, / one is freed from all sins, like the moon from Rāhu.
The two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara are on the southern bank of the Yamunā; / having bathed there and drunk [the water], one is freed from all sins.
Having gone there to that place of wise Mahādeva, / a man delivers all—ten past [ancestors] and ten future [descendants].
Performing bathing there, a man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice; / he attains the world of heaven until the dissolution of beings.
On the eastern side of the Gaṅgā, famed in the three worlds, O Bhārata, / is the well called Sāmudra, and the famous Pratiṣṭhāna.
If a celibate who has conquered anger stays there for three nights, / purified in soul of all sins, he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
To the north of Pratiṣṭhāna, but to the east of the Bhāgīrathī, / is the holy place named Haṃsaprapatana, renowned across the three worlds.
Merely by bathing in it, O Bhārata, there is the fruit of a horse sacrifice; / as long as the moon and the sun exist, so long is he exalted in heaven.
Whoever, free from malice, satisfies the ancestors with water / on the pleasant, broad sandbank of Urvaśī, pale as a swan,
for sixty thousand years and sixty hundreds of years / he enjoys the world of heaven together with his ancestors, O ruler of men.
He is constantly worshipped there by sages, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras; / then, having fallen from heaven, his karma exhausted, dropped from the sky,
he obtains a hundred maidens resembling Urvaśī, / and becomes the enjoyer of hundreds of thousands of cows, O king.
Awakened from sleep by the sound of girdles and anklets, / having enjoyed extensive pleasures, he reaches that holy place again.
Always holding a seat of kuśa grass, self-restrained, with senses subdued, / eating only once a day for a month, he becomes a master of enjoyment.
He obtains a hundred women adorned with gold; / on earth up to the ocean, he becomes a lord of great enjoyment.
He becomes an enjoyer of ten thousand villages, a king; / endowed with wealth and grain, he becomes a perpetual giver.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, he remembers that holy place again. / Now at that pleasant banyan tree, a celibate with conquered senses,
fasting and engaged in yoga, would attain knowledge of Brahman. / Having reached Koṭitīrtha, whoever abandons his life
is exalted in the world of heaven for thousands of crores of years; / then, having fallen from heaven, his karma exhausted, dropped from the sky,
he is born handsome in a family rich in gold, jewels, and pearls. / Then, having gone to Bhogavatī, to the north of Vāsuki,
there is another holy place there, Daśāśvamedhaka. / Performing bathing there, a man obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
he becomes rich in wealth, handsome, capable, generous, and righteous. / Whatever merit is in the four Vedas, whatever fruit among truth-speakers,
and whatever dharma is in non-violence—that accrues merely by going there. / The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever it is plunged into;
ten times greater than Kurukṣetra where it meets the Sindhu; / where the highly blessed Gaṅgā possesses many holy places and wealth of asceticism.
For it should be known as a field of perfection; no doubt should be entertained here. / It carries mortals across on earth, and also carries the Nāgas across below;
it carries the gods across in heaven; therefore it is traditionally called Tripathā. / As long as the bones of an embodied being remain in the Gaṅgā,
for so many thousands of years is he honored in the world of heaven. / It is the supreme pilgrimage site among sacred places, the highest river among rivers,
granting liberation to all beings, even to those who have committed great sins. / The Gaṅgā is easily reached everywhere, [but] difficult of access at three places:
at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence with the ocean. / Bathing there, they go to heaven; those who die [there] have no rebirth.
And for all beings whose minds are afflicted by sin, / seeking a destination, there is no destination equal to the Gaṅgā.
She who is the purest of the pure, the most auspicious of auspicious things, / fallen from Maheśvara's head, removing all sin, auspicious.

3.44.m: Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Hear once again, O King, the glorification of Prayāga, / by hearing which one is freed from all sins, there is no doubt about this.
There is a sacred place named Mānasa on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā. / Having fasted for three nights [there], one would attain all desires.
Whatever fruit a man obtains through the gift of cows, land, and gold, / he obtains this [same] fruit if he again remembers that sacred place.
Whether free of desire or full of desire, whoever dies in the Gaṅgā, / dead, he enters heaven and does not see hell.
Asleep, he is awakened by the songs of groups of apsarases; / he travels on an aerial chariot yoked with swans and sārusa cranes.
For many years, O best of kings, they enjoy six thousand [years]; / then, fallen from heaven, his karma exhausted, dropped from the sky,
he is born into an illustrious family rich in gold, jewels, and pearls. / Sixty thousand sacred places and six hundred sacred places
go to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the month of Māgha. / Whatever is the fruit of one hundred thousand cows given properly,
that is the fruit of bathing for three days at Prayāga in the month of Māgha. / But whoever practices the five fires between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
having all limbs intact, free from disease, and possessed of the five senses— / as many hair follicles as the body of that embodied being has,
for so many thousands of years he is honored in the world of heaven. / Then, fallen from heaven, he becomes the ruler of Jambūdvīpa.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, that man worships that sacred place. / Whoever enters the water at the world-renowned confluence,
like the moon seized by Rāhu [and then released], freed from all sins, / he attains the world of the Moon and rejoices with Soma.
For sixty thousand and six hundred years / he attains the world of heaven, served by sages and gandharvas.
Falling from there, O best of kings, he is born into a prosperous family. / And a man who, head downwards and feet upwards, drinks the flame,
for one hundred thousand years is honored in the world of heaven. / Falling from there, O best of kings, the man becomes an agnihotrin.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, that man worships that sacred place. / But whoever, cutting up his body, gives it to birds,
hear also the fruit of him who is consumed by birds: / for one hundred thousand years he is honored in the world of the Moon.
Then, fallen from heaven, he becomes a righteous king, / virtuous, endowed with beauty, learned, and possessing an attractive body.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, he again worships that sacred place. / On the northern bank of the Yamunā and to the south of Prayāga,
there is a supreme sacred place traditionally called Ṛṇapramocana. / Having stayed for one night [there], one is freed from all debts;
he attains the world of the Sun and becomes free of debt forever.

3.45.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Having heard this praise of Prayāga that was recited by you, / this heart has become purified from the recitation of Prayāga. / Tell me, O venerable one, what is the fruit of fasting to death there?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Hear, O King, O lord, what kind of fruit of fasting to death at Prayāga / a wise and faithful person obtains:
with limbs intact, free of disease, and possessed of all five senses, / the fruit of a horse sacrifice is his at every step as he goes.
He would deliver ten ancestral families before and ten after, O King; / he is freed from all sins and goes to the supreme state.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / You are fortunate, O knower of dharma; tell me about giving, O lord, / by which with very little effort one may obtain many merits.
A horse sacrifice is obtained here [only] by many meritorious deeds. / Resolve this doubt of mine; my curiosity is indeed great.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Hear, O King, O great hero, what was spoken by the lotus-born [Brahmā]; / as it was being told long ago in the presence of the sages, it was heard by me.
The circle of Prayāga extends five yojanas; / for one entering upon its land, there is a horse sacrifice at every step.
Seven past generations of men and fourteen future generations / a man delivers—all of them—who abandons his life [there].
Knowing thus, O best of kings, one should always be devoted to faith. / Faithless men whose minds are stricken by sin / do not reach that place, Prayāga, created by the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / But those who, out of attachment or greed for wealth, have succumbed to desire— / what is their fruit of the pilgrimage site? How might they obtain merit?
For one who sells all kinds of merchandise, not knowing what is proper to do or not to do, / what is his destiny at Prayāga? Tell me this, O great sage.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Hear, O King, the great secret that destroys all sins: / if a person resides at Prayāga for a month with senses controlled, O best of kings,
he is freed from all sins, just as ordained by the Self-born. / Becoming pure, self-controlled, non-violent, and endowed with faith,
he is freed from all sins and goes to the supreme state. / But hear the fruit at Prayāga for betrayers of trust:
one should bathe at all three times of day and sustain oneself on alms; / after three months one would be freed at Prayāga, there is no doubt.
And he whose pilgrimage and other rites here are done with wisdom / is endowed with all desires and is honored in the world of heaven.
He obtains a permanent abode filled with wealth and grain; / thus filled with wisdom, he always enjoys pleasures.

His ancestors and great-grandfathers are delivered by him from hell. / In accordance with dharma, O knower of truth, as you ask again and again, / this eternal secret has been declared for your pleasure.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Today my birth has borne fruit; today my family has borne fruit! / I am pleased and favored today simply by the sight of you. / By the sight of you, O righteous one, I have been freed from all sins.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / By good fortune your birth has borne fruit; by good fortune your family has been delivered. / From recitation merit increases; when heard, it destroys sin.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / But what is the merit, what is the fruit at the Yamunā, O great sage? / Relate all this to me just as it has been seen and heard.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / The divine daughter of the Sun is renowned in the three worlds, / the fortunate river Yamunā, where she arrives.
By whichever [way] the Gaṅgā issued forth, by that same [way] went the Yamunā. / Across thousands of leagues, by being recited, she destroys sins.
Having bathed there and drank [the water] of the Yamunā, O Yudhiṣṭhira, / through recitation one gains merit, and upon seeing [her], one beholds blessings.
Bathed in and drank from, she purifies up to the seventh generation of a family. / Whoever casts off his breath of life there goes to the highest destination.
On the southern bank of the Yamunā is the well-known Agnitīrtha. / To the west, the holy place of Dharmarāja is considered an excellent boon of Hara.
Having bathed there, they go to heaven; those who die there suffer no rebirth. / Thus are the thousands of holy places on the southern bank of the Yamunā.
I shall declare [those] to the north of the high-souled Āditya: / the holy place named Viraja, where the gods together with Vāsava
used to worship the twilight constantly, O Yudhiṣṭhira. / The gods serve that holy place, as do other wise men.
Becoming filled with faith, perform ablutions at the holy place. / There are also many other auspicious holy places that remove all sins.
Having bathed in them, they go to heaven; those who die there suffer no rebirth. / Both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are recorded as having equal fruit.
Solely on account of her preeminent nature, the Gaṅgā is worshipped everywhere. / In this manner, O son of Kuntī, perform ablutions at the holy place of heaven.
The sin committed over a lifetime is destroyed that very instant. / But whoever, rising at dawn, recites or hears this
is freed from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.

3.46.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / I have heard what was proclaimed by Brahmā in the Purāṇa, commensurate with merit, / about the thousands, hundreds, and myriads of holy places.
All are meritorious and pure, and considered the supreme destination. / On earth, Naimiṣa is meritorious, and in the atmosphere, Puṣkara.
Kurukṣetra is distinguished even above Prayāga for the worlds. / Having abandoned all of them, how do you praise just one?
This which has been proclaimed is unauthoritative, unbelievable, [though declared] unexcelled: / the supreme, divine destination and desired pleasures as one wishes.
Why do you praise great duty through little yoga? / Explain this doubt to me just as it has been seen and heard.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / What is unbelievable should not be spoken, even if it be directly perceived, / to a man of faith whose mind has been struck down by sin.
For the faithless is impure, evil-minded, and bereft of auspiciousness. / All these are sinners; therefore this was spoken by me.
Hear the glorification of Prayāga just as it has been seen and heard, / both directly perceived and beyond perception, and as other [things] will come to be.
Just as other [things] were seen by me formerly, O king, and just as they were heard: / having made the scripture the authority, one's own yoga is revered.
Another suffers there and would not attain yoga at all. / Only after thousands of other births is yoga attained by mortals.
Just as yoga is attained by mortals through a thousand yogas, / he who gives all gems to the Brahmins—
by that gift bestowed, yoga is attained by mortals. / For one who has died at Prayāga, all this comes to pass, not otherwise.
I shall declare the primary cause to those who have faith, O Bhārata. / Just as in all beings and everywhere indeed is seen
brahman—there is nothing at all [else], which is why this is said: / just as brahman is worshipped everywhere in all beings,
so in all the worlds Prayāga is worshipped by the wise. / The king of holy places is worshipped; this is the truth, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Even Brahmā constantly remembers the excellent holy place Prayāga. / Having reached the king of holy places, he desires nothing else at all.
For who, having attained godhood, would wish to become human? / By this very inference you will know, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Whether merit or demerit, it has been told by me just as it is. / Yudhiṣṭhira said: / That which has been spoken by you has been heard; I am amazed again and again.
How is attainment of that [brought about] by yoga, whereas the heavenly world is [gained] by action? / Then one also obtains pleasures, and the earth as the fruit of those actions.
I ask again about those actions by which the earth is obtained. / Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Hear, O strong-armed king, how the earth [is gained] by the action as described.
A cow, fire, a Brahmin, scripture, gold, water, women, / a mother, and a father: whoever censures [these], O ruler of men,
for them there is no upward movement; thus said Prajāpati. / Thus is the attainment of yoga, the exceedingly rare state.
Those men who are evil-doers go to a terrible hell. / An elephant, a horse, a cow, an ox, gems, pearls and so forth, gold—
whoever steals [these] out of sight and later bestows a gift: / they do not go to heaven, where givers enjoy pleasures.
Joined with such an action, the base are cooked in hell. / Thus [concerning] yoga, duty, and the giver, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
as whether it is true or untrue, whether it exists or does not exist, whatever the fruit, / I shall proclaim the explanation, so that he may attain it himself.

3.47.m: Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Hear again, O king, the glorification of Prayāga: / Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara, Gotīrtha, the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean,
Kurukṣetra, and Gayā, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, / and these and many other holy mountains—
ten thousand holy places, and likewise thirty crores of others / are perpetually situated at Prayāga; so say the wise.
And there are three fire-altar pits, in the midst of which the Gaṅgā, / honored by all holy places, has issued forth from Prayāga.
The divine daughter of the Sun, renowned in the three worlds, / the Gaṅgā along with the Yamunā, remains cherishing the world.
Between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is considered the hips of the earth. / [Other holy places] do not equal a sixteenth part of Prayāga, O tiger among kings.
Vāyu declared there are three and a half crores of holy places; / whether in heaven, on earth, or in the atmosphere, all that is considered the Gaṅgā.
Prayāga is the settlement, both Kambala and Aśvatara, / and that which is Bhogavatī: this is the sacrificial altar of Prajāpati.
There the gods and the sacrifices, embodied, O Yudhiṣṭhira, / worship Prayāga, and [so do] the sages rich in austerities.
Kings with abundant wealth worship the gods with sacrifices. / Therefore nothing is more meritorious in the three worlds, O Bhārata.
By its power, O lord, it surpasses all holy places: / ten thousand holy places, and likewise three crores of others.
Where the glorious Gaṅgā is, that region is an ascetic grove; / that should be known as a field of perfection, resting on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
This truth he should whisper into the ear of twice-born men, of holy persons, of his son, / of his friends, or of a devoted pupil.
This brings prosperity; this leads to heaven; this is worthy of resort; this is auspicious. / This is meritorious; this is delightful, purifying, the highest dharma.
This secret of the great seers destroys all sins. / Having studied it and meditating upon it, a twice-born achieves spotless purity.
And whoever, ever pure, constantly listens to [the glory of] this holy pilgrimage site, / attains memory of past births and rejoices on the crest of heaven.
Those sacred pilgrimage sites are to be reached by the virtuous who perceive what is proper. / Bathe in the sacred sites, descendant of Kuru, and do not be perverse in mind!
When asked properly by you, O lord, it has been told by me. / All the ancestors have been delivered, and the grandfathers have been delivered.
Yet all of them are not worth a sixteenth part of Prayāga. / Thus knowledge, yoga, and pilgrimage sites, O Yudhiṣṭhira—
they are joined with much hardship, and from that they go to the highest goal. / But by the mere remembrance of Prayāga, a person goes to the heavenly world.

3.48.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / This whole account of Prayāga has been told, O great sage. / In the same way, tell me all about how it may deliver me.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / Listen, O king, I shall speak; this entire world has been described. / Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Īśāna—the deity, the imperishable Lord:
Brahmā creates beings, whatever is immobile and mobile; / Viṣṇu protects those creatures in the other world.
At the end of the kalpa, Rudra indeed destroys that entire world. / He does not bestow, nor does he reflect, nor does he ever perish.
He is the Lord of all beings; he who sees [this] sees truly. / North of Pratiṣṭhāna, Brahmā now abides.
Having become the banyan tree, the supreme lord Maheśvara resides there; / and thereupon the gods along with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and the great seers
constantly protect that supreme [abode] from those devoted to sinful acts; / and those others who abide [here] do not go to the highest goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Tell me according to truth how their tradition stands; / or for what reason do those revered by the world abide here?
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / These three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—dwell in Prayāga. / But I shall declare the reason; listen to the truth, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The circle of Prayāga extends five yojanas. / They stand to protect it, warding off sinful actions,
lest even a tiny sin committed therein should cast one down into hell. / In this way, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are at Prayāga.
The seven continents, the oceans, and the mountains on the earth / stand supported until the dissolution of beings.
And whatever many others there are, all stand [here], O Yudhiṣṭhira; / starting from the earth's site, it was fashioned by the three deities.
This is the sacred domain of Prajāpati, celebrated as Prayāga. / This Prayāga, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is meritorious and purifying.
Rule your own kingdom, O king of kings, together with your brothers!

3.49.m: Sūta said: / All the Pāṇḍavas, resolute in dharma, together with their brothers, / bowed to the brāhmaṇas and propitiated the gurus and the gods.
Then Vāsudeva too arrived there in a moment; / that Mādhava was worshipped by all the Pāṇḍavas together.
Together with all those great-souled ones and with Kṛṣṇa, / Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was consecrated again in his own kingdom.
And in the meantime, the great-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, / having spoken 'May there be welfare!', went in an instant to his hermitage.
And the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers— / that son of Dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, then distributed great gifts.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, reads or listens to this, / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Vāsudeva said: / My word must be followed; I speak out of affection for you: / Constantly devoted to sacrifice, free from anguish at Prayāga,
always remembering Prayāga together with us, O Yudhiṣṭhira, / you yourself, O king of kings, will attain the eternal realm of heaven.
Whatever person follows Prayāga or dwells there, / with mind purified of all sin, goes to the heavenly world.
Turned away from accepting gifts, contented, restrained, pure,

and free from egoism, he enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford. / Free from anger, O king of kings, speaking truth, firm in vows, / and regarding creatures as himself, he enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.
Sacrifices were declared by the seers, and also by the gods in due order. / These sacrifices cannot indeed be performed by a poor man, O protector of the earth.
A sacrifice requires many implements, with a flurry of various provisions; / it is undertaken by varied wealthy men, or rarely by prosperous people.
That which can be attained even by the wise who are poor, O lord of men, / through sacred fruits of sacrifice—learn of that, O lord of people!
This is the supreme secret of the seers, O best of the Bharatas: / holy pilgrimage to sacred places is superior even to sacrifices.
A hundred million, and thirty crores besides, / will go to the Gaṅgā in the month of Māgha, O bull among men.
Be at ease, O great king, having enjoyed the thornless kingdom! / You will see [it] again, O king of kings, especially as a sacrificer.

3.50.m: The seers said: / Everything that was asked has indeed been told by you. / Now we ask again; tell us one thing, O highly intelligent one!
What fruit one obtains from resorting to these sacred places— / by performing what single act can it be obtained for all of them?
Tell us this, O omniscient one, if such an action exists. / Sūta said: / The yoga of action is indeed declared for the castes, beginning with the twice-born.
It is of various kinds, O blessed ones, and among them one excels: / by whomsoever devotion to Hari is performed in mind, speech, and voice,
by him victory is won, by him victory is won; it is won indeed, without a doubt! / Hari alone is to be worshipped, the Lord of all lords of gods.
By the great mantras of the name of Hari, the goblin of sin will perish. / Having circumambulated Hari even once with pure intentions,
they attain the immersion of all sacred fords; there is no doubt about this. / And having beheld the image of Hari, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords.
Having chanted the supreme name of Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit of all mantras. / Having smelled the tulasī from the prasāda of Viṣṇu, O best of the twice-born,
one does not see that fierce and terrifying mouth of Yama. / One who bows once to Kṛṣṇa will never drink the mother's breast-milk.
Perpetual homage unto those whose mind is fixed on the feet of Hari! / Be they Pulkasa or Śvapaca, or whatever other outcast classes,
even they are venerable, highly blessed, if they serve only the feet of Hari; / how much more then the holy brāhmaṇas, the devotees, and likewise the royal seers!
Having simply offered devotion to Hari, one never experiences dwelling in a womb. / A man who dances before Hari with loud sounds, chanting His name,
purifies the world, O brāhmaṇas, like the waters of the Gaṅgā and other [sacred rivers]. / From seeing him, touching him, or speaking with him out of devotion,
one is freed from sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt. / A man who circumambulates Hari while loudly chanting his name,
clapping his hands and the like in sweet and melodious sounds, / claps away sin such as killing a brāhmaṇa by that very act.
And whoever, having recited stories of devotion to Hari, hears [such] a narrative, / by merely seeing him, a human being becomes pure.
What doubt, then, can there be regarding his sins, O best of sages? / And the name of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme sacred place among sacred places, O great sages.
Those who have taken the name of Kṛṣṇa make the earth a sacred place. / Therefore, O best of sages, the wise know of no greater merit than this.
Having eaten the remnants of offerings to Viṣṇu and placing them on his head, / a mortal becomes Viṣṇu himself, destroying sorrow and Yama.
Hari alone is to be worshipped and saluted, without doubt. / Those who see the unmanifest Mahāviṣṇu or the god Maheśvara
as one have no rebirth; / therefore [one should worship] Viṣṇu, the imperishable Self without beginning or end.
and Hari—as one, and worship [him] just so. / Those who regard Hari and another deity as equal,
they go to terrible hells; a wise man should not even count them. / Whether a fool or a scholar, a brāhmaṇa dear to Keśava,
or an outcaste, Lord Nārāyaṇa himself liberates him. / There is no forest fire for the heap of sins higher than Nārāyaṇa.
Even after committing a terrible sin, one is liberated through the name of Kṛṣṇa. / The divine Nārāyaṇa himself, the teacher of the worlds, has placed
in his own name a power greater than himself, O [sages] of good vows. / Here, those who dispute this, seeing the effort as slight
and yet the fruits as weighty, go to many hells. / Therefore, one should be devoted to Hari, dedicated to Hari's name.
The Lord protects his worshipper from behind, and the chanter of his name at his breast. / The name of Hari is a great thunderbolt in splitting the mountain of sin.
His two feet are fruitful which walk for Hari's sake; / those two hands alone are declared blessed which perform [his] worship.
That head is the best head which bows down to Hari; / that is a tongue which praises Hari; that is a mind which follows his feet.
And those bodily hairs are spoken of [as true hairs] which stand on end at his name; / and that is tear-water which flows on account of Acyuta.
Alas! People are utterly deceived through the fault of destiny! / They do not worship him who grants liberation by the mere utterance of his name.
They are deceived and corrupted by association with women, / whose body hair does not stand on end at the sound of ‘Kṛṣṇa’!
They are fools, undisciplined souls, agitated by grief for sons and the like; / they weep with many lamentations, but not in chanting the syllables of Kṛṣṇa['s name].
Even having obtained a tongue in this world, one does not chant the name of Kṛṣṇa; / even having obtained the ladder to liberation, they fall away out of mere negligence.
Therefore, with effort indeed, a man [should worship] Viṣṇu through karmayoga. / Viṣṇu, when worshipped through karmayoga, is pleased; not otherwise.
The worship of Viṣṇu is said to be a sacred place superior to any sacred place. / Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by bathing, drinking, and plunging
at all the sacred places, that fruit [he obtains] from the service of Kṛṣṇa. / Blessed indeed are the men who worship Hari through karmayoga.
Therefore, O sages, worship Kṛṣṇa, the supreme auspiciousness.

3.51.m: The sages said: / How is karmayoga [performed], O Sūta, and by what is Hari propitiated / so that he is pleased? O highly fortunate one, best of speakers, tell us,
how that blessed Lord is to be worshipped by seekers of liberation; / tell that, which protects all the worlds and is the summary of dharma.
Tell us of that karmayoga, O Sūta, which is embodied; / thus the brāhmaṇas, desiring to hear, stand before you.
Sūta said: / Thus formerly was Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, questioned / by the sages resembling fire; Vyāsa said to them—hear that:
Vyāsa said: / Hear, all you sages, the eternal [path] to be spoken, / karmayoga, which gives ultimate fruit to brāhmaṇas.
All that is established by the Vedas has been shown for the sake of brāhmaṇas. / Formerly, while the sages listened, Manu Prajāpati declared it,
which removes all afflictions, is meritorious, and is practiced by groups of sages. / With collected minds, hear while I speak:

Having undergone the sacred thread investiture, the best of the twice-born should study the Vedas, / in the eighth year from conception or the eighth year [from birth], according to the rule declared in his own sūtra.
Bearing a staff, wearing a girdle and sacred thread, wearing a black antelope skin, like a sage, / living on alms-food, intent on the guru's welfare, gazing at the guru's face,
made of cotton for the sacred thread formerly fashioned by Brahmā, / a triple-cord for brāhmaṇas, or of kuśa grass, or made of cloth.
A twice-born should always wear the sacred thread, and always have his topknot tied; / otherwise, whatever rite is done becomes as though undone.
He should wear an uncorrupted garment, cotton or ochre-dyed; / that very garment should be worn, white, woven, [and] of superior quality.
The upper garment is traditionally taught to be an auspicious black antelope skin; / in its absence, [the skin] of a cow, or of a ruru deer, is prescribed.
Lifting the right arm, placed over the left arm, / it is always upavīta; when hanging around the neck, [it is] nivīta.
Lifting the left arm, worn on the right, O twice-born, / it is called prācīnāvīta; one should employ it in ancestral rites.
In the fire-sanctuary, in the cow pen, at a burnt offering, and likewise at penance, / during daily Vedic recitation, at meals, and in the presence of brāhmaṇas,
during attendance on gurus, at the two twilights, and in the company of the virtuous, / he should always wear the sacred thread; this is the eternal rule.
A brāhmaṇa's girdle should be made of triple, smooth, intertwined muñja grass; / in the absence of muñja, they say it should be of kuśa grass, with one knot or three.
A twice-born should hold a staff made of bamboo or palāśa reaching to the hair, / or born of a tree fit for sacrifice, pleasant, and without flaws.
Morning and evening, the twice-born should worship the twilight with a concentrated mind; / if he abandons it out of desire, greed, fear, or delusion, he becomes fallen.
Then, with a cheerful mind, he should perform the fire-ritual morning and evening; / having bathed, he should offer libations to the gods, sages, and groups of ancestors.
He should worship the deities with flowers, leaves, barley, and water; / he should habitually greet elders with respect according to dharma,
with a complete prostration, saying: 'I am so-and-so by name, sir,' / for the attainment of long life and health, free from drowsiness and the like.
The brāhmaṇa [elder] should say in response to the greeting: 'May you be long-lived, gentle one,' / and the sound 'a' at the end of his name should be pronounced with the preceding vowel protracted.
The brāhmaṇa who does not know the return greeting to a salutation / should not be greeted by a learned man; he is just like a śūdra.
The clasping of the guru's feet should be done with crossed hands: / the left foot should be touched with the left [hand], and the right with the right.
Having obtained knowledge—whether worldly, Vedic, or spiritual—/ from him, one should, being pure, salute him first.
One should not carry water, alms-food, flowers, and fuel sticks, / nor similar things, during rituals meant for the gods.
One should inquire of a brāhmaṇa’s welfare (kuśala), of a kṣatriya’s health (anāmaya), / of a vaiśya’s prosperity (kṣema) upon meeting him, and of a śūdra’s good health (ārogya).
The teacher, father, elder brother, protector from fear, / maternal uncle, father-in-law, and maternal and paternal grandfathers,
a superior in caste, and a paternal uncle are considered elders (guru) for a man here. / Mother, maternal grandmother, the guru’s wife, and sisters of father and mother,
mother-in-law, paternal grandmother, elder sister, and nurse are the female elders. / O twice-born, this group of elders is to be known through mother and father.
One should attend to them with mind, speech, and bodily actions. / Seeing the elders, one should rise, bow respectfully, with hands folded in reverent salutation.
One should not sit with them, nor argue for one's own sake. / Even for the sake of one's life, one must never speak out of hatred toward elders.
Though abundant in other virtues, one who hates an elder falls low. / Even among all elders, five are to be worshipped especially.
Of these, the first three are best, and among them the mother is most honoured: / he who supports, she who gives birth, he by whom knowledge is taught,
the elder brother, and the husband—these five are considered elders. / By oneself, with all effort, or even by sacrificing one’s life,
these five are to be worshipped especially by one who desires prosperity. / As long as father and mother, these two, are free from impairment,
so long should a son abandon everything and be devoted to them. / If father and mother are thoroughly pleased with the qualities of their son,
that son obtains all dharma through that deed. / There is no deity equal to a mother; there is no elder equal to a father.
A return of their favour is not possible in any way. / One should always do what is dear to them by deed, mind, and speech.
Without being permitted by the two of them, one should not perform another dharma, / except for that which has liberation as its fruit, and also the regular and occasional [duties].
This essence of dharma is declared to grant infinite fruit after death. / Having properly honoured the instructor, sent off with his permission,
the student enjoys the fruit of knowledge and after death goes to heaven. / The fool who despises his elder brother who is equal to a father,
by that fault, having died, goes to a terrible hell. / In the way established for men, the husband is always to be worshipped.
Even over a mother, the husband's weightiness in this world arises from his benefaction. / Maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests, and teachers:
Rising to meet them, he should say, 'I am so-and-so,' and salute them. / An initiated person should not be addressed by name, even if he is younger.
One who knows dharma should address him with 'bhoḥ' or 'bhavat' beforehand. / He is to be greeted, worshipped, and bowed to with the head
by brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and others who desire prosperity, always respectfully. / But kṣatriyas and others must never be saluted [first] by a vipra.
Even if they are endowed with knowledge, virtuous conduct, and are very learned, / the brāhmaṇa should pronounce 'svasti' to all the castes—so says the scripture.
A greeting is certainly to be made by an equal in caste to equals in caste. / Fire is the guru of the twice-born; the brāhmaṇa is the guru of the castes;
the husband alone is the guru of women; a guest is a guru everywhere. / Knowledge, action, age, kin, and wealth is the fifth:
they say these are the five grounds of respect, each earlier one weightier than the later. / In the three castes, whoever possesses more of the five
is worthy of respect here; even a śūdra who has reached his tenth decade. / The road should be yielded to a brāhmaṇa, to a woman, to a king, to a blind man,
to an old man, to one broken under a burden, to a sick person, and to a weak man. / Having gathered alms from the houses of virtuous people daily with self-control,

and having offered it to the guru, he should eat with his permission, restrained in speech. / The best of the twice-born, wearing the sacred thread, should beg for alms with 'bhavat' at the beginning;
a kṣatriya with 'bhavat' in the middle, but a vaiśya with 'bhavat' at the end. / From one's mother, or sister, or own mother's sister,
he should beg for alms first, [from one] who would not disregard him. / At houses of the same caste, or from all castes,
the practice of begging alms is prescribed, avoiding fallen persons and the like, / from those not devoid of the Vedas and sacrifices, who are praiseworthy in their duties.
A student (brahmacārin) should daily bring alms from houses with self-control. / He should not beg at the guru's family, nor among the families of kinsmen or relatives.
However, in the absence of other houses, he should avoid each earlier one. / Or he may wander through the whole village if the aforementioned are unavailable,
restraining his speech, pure, and not looking about the directions. / Having collected alms-food only as much as needed, without deceit,
he should eat, pure, always restrained in speech, with undivided mind. / He should constantly subsist on alms-food; one under a vow should never eat food from a single house.
The livelihood of one subsisting on alms-food is considered equal to fasting. / One should always honour food, and eat it without reviling it.
Seeing it, one should rejoice, be pleased, and welcome it in every way. / Overeating causes illness, shortens life, prevents heaven,
is unmeritorious, and is detested by the world; therefore, one should avoid it. / Facing east one should eat foods, or facing the sun;
one should never eat facing north—this is the eternal rule. / Having washed hands and feet, before eating he should sip water twice;
seated in a clean place, and having eaten, he should sip water twice.

3.52.m: Vyāsa said: / Having eaten, drunk, slept, bathed, and when walking on a street, / having touched his lips and body hair, and having put on clothes improperly,
upon the emission of semen, urine, and feces, when speaking a falsehood, / after spitting, at the beginning of Vedic study, and upon coughing or shortness of breath,
or having entered a crossroad or a cremation ground, the best of the twice-born, / similarly at both twilight rituals, even if he has already sipped water, should sip water again.
When conversing with a caṇḍāla or a mleccha, or speaking to a woman, śūdra, or an impure person, / having seen an impure person or food of that kind,
one should sip water; or upon the falling of tears, or likewise of blood; / at a meal, at the two twilights, having bathed, having drunk, after urine and feces,
or having come, having slept, he should sip water once, or once more from another [cause]. / At the touching of fire or cows, or having touched a pure person,
or on the touching of women or oneself, or having worn blue cloth and the like, / he should touch water, or grass, or the earth.
On touching his own hair, or when his garment has slipped down, / with water that is not hot, free from hairs, unpolluted, and according to rule,
for purification, he should always sip water while seated, facing east or north. / Having covered his head or his neck, or with his hair or crest untied,
without having washed his feet, he does not become pure according to the rule. / Wearing shoes, or standing in shoes, or wearing a turban, a wise man should not sip water;
nor with streams of rain, nor standing up with water drawn up, / nor with water poured with one hand, or without the sacred thread;
nor seated on sandals, or with his knees placed outside [his garment], / nor while talking, laughing, looking about, or lying on a bed;
nor with waters that are not inspected, or accompanied by foam and the like, / nor with waters released by the hand of a śūdra or an impure person, nor with saline waters.
And he should not make a sound with his fingers, nor be distracted in mind, / nor [sip water] corrupted by color or taste, nor water from a chasm,
nor [water] agitated by the hand, nor [water having] an external smell. / A brahmin is purified by [water] reaching the heart, a kṣatriya is purified by [water reaching] the throat,
likewise a vaiśya by [water] that is tasted, and a woman or a śūdra by touching [the lips] at the end. / The [tīrtha] inside the base of the thumb on the line is called the Brāhma tīrtha;
the tīrtha of the ancestors is said to be between the thumb and forefinger. / Behind the base of the little finger, they declare the Prājāpatya tīrtha.
The tip of the fingers is considered the Daiva tīrtha; that same is proclaimed as the Ārṣa. / At the base it is Daiva and Ārṣa, and in the middle it is remembered as Āgneya;
that same is the Saumika tīrtha. Knowing this, one is not bewildered. / A twice-born should always perform the sipping of water using only the Brāhma tīrtha;
or he may offer oblations with the Daiva, but never with that of the ancestors, O twice-born. / First, he should attentively drink water three times with the Brāhma tīrtha;
then, having wiped it with the base of the thumb, he should touch the mouth. / Then, with the thumb and ring finger, he should touch the two eyes;
with the contact of forefinger and thumb he should touch the two nostrils; / with the contact of little finger and thumb he should touch the ears;
and with the contact of all [fingers] he should touch the heart or the body; / likewise he should touch the head, and with the thumb the two shoulders.
When he drinks the water three times, the deities Brahmā, Viṣṇu, / and Maheśa are pleased with him by that, so we have heard.
From wiping [the mouth], the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are pleased. / When the two eyes are touched, the moon and the sun are pleased.
He should touch the two nostrils: the Nāsatyas and Dasras are pleased. / Likewise, when the two ears are touched, wind and fire are pleased.
And when his heart is touched, all the deities are pleased. / From touching the crown of the head, that person becomes unique and delighted.
Drops that cling to the body do not make one impure at the mouth; / [food] stuck in the teeth is like the teeth—upon contact with the tongue, one becomes pure.
The drops that touch the feet of one who is causing others to sip water / should be known as equal to dust on the ground; by them there is no impurity.
At the madhuparka and soma, and when eating betel, / [and with] fruit, roots, and sugarcane, Manu declared no fault.
If a man, while moving about during food and drink, should have an article in his hand, / he should place that article on the ground, sip water, and then sprinkle it [with water].
If a twice-born, having taken a metallic vessel, should become impure with food remnants, / he should place that article on the ground, sip water, and then sprinkle it [with water].
Whatever article he has taken when he becomes possessed of food remnants, / without placing that article on the ground, he would go to impurity.
Regarding clothes and the like there is an option: having touched it, he should sip water here. / In a wilderness, in a deserted place, at night, or on a path filled with thieves and tigers,
having passed urine or feces with an article in hand, he is not defiled. / Having placed the sacred thread on his right ear, facing north,
he should pass feces and urine by day, but facing south at night, / having covered the earth with pieces of wood, leaves, a clod of earth, or grass,
and having covered his head, he should perform the discharge of feces and urine. / In shade, near a well, a river, a cow-pen, a sacred tree, water, paths, ashes,
and in fire, and in a cremation ground, he must not pass feces and urine; / neither on cow dung, nor on wood, nor near a great tree, nor on grass;
not standing, nor unclothed, nor on a mountain range; / not in a ruined temple, and never on an anthill;
not in pits with living creatures, nor walking along must he do so; / on chaff, charcoal, potsherds, and likewise on the king's highway;
not in a field, nor in a hole, nor at a sacred ford, nor at a crossroad; / nor in a garden, nor near water, nor in saline ground, nor in a city reservoir;
nor wearing shoes or wooden sandals, nor holding an umbrella, nor in the open air; / and never facing women, a guru, a brahmin, or cows;
never facing a deity, a temple, or water; / nor looking at the celestial lights, nor facing them;
likewise facing the sun, facing fire, or facing the moon. / Having gathered clay from a riverbank, which removes smear and odor,
unwearied, he should perform purification with pure water drawn out [of a reservoir]. / A brahmin should not collect clay that is dusty or muddy,
nor from a road, nor from saline ground, nor what is left over from another's purification, / nor from a temple, a well, a house, and likewise not from water.
Then he should always sip water according to the rule declared previously.

3.53.m: Vyāsa said: / Thus equipped with a staff and the rest, endowed with purification and good conduct, / summoned, he should study while looking at the face of the guru.
He should always have hands raised, be of virtuous conduct, and well restrained; / and when told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the guru.
He should not respond or converse while lying down, / nor sitting, nor eating, nor standing, nor with his face turned away.
His bed and seat must always be lower in the presence of the guru; / within the range of the guru's sight, he must not sit as he pleases.
He should not pronounce his name, even when he is out of sight, / and he should not imitate his gait, speech, or gestures.
Where censure or slander of the guru takes place, / the two ears must be covered there, or he should go elsewhere from that place.
Standing far off, he should not venerate him, nor when angry, nor near a woman; / and he must not contradict him, nor sit near him while standing.
He should always fetch for him a water pot, kuśa grass, flowers, and firewood; / he should always perform cleansing and anointing of his limbs.
He should never step on his discarded flower garland, bed, wooden sandals, or shoes, / nor on his seat, nor on his shadow and the like.
He should procure tooth-sticks and the like, and present whatever is obtained to him; / he should not depart without asking leave, and must be devoted to what is agreeable and beneficial.
He must never stretch out his feet in his presence; / yawning, laughing, and covering the throat,
and cracking the knuckles he should always avoid in his presence. / He should study at the proper time as long as the guru is not dispirited.
Sitting below at the side of the guru, well concentrated on service, / he should never remain on a seat, bed, or vehicle [together with him].
