When he runs, he should run after him; when he walks, he walks behind him; / on a carriage drawn by bullocks, horses, or camels, in a palace, and on low seats,
and on a rock, a wooden board, or in boats, he may sit together with the guru. / He should constantly master his senses, be self-controlled, free from anger, and pure.
He should always use speech that is sweet and beneficial. / Perfume, flower garlands, tasty food, fermented drink, pearl oyster, harming living beings,
anointing, collyrium, massaging, holding an umbrella, / lust, greed, fear, sleep, singing, instrumental music, dancing,
threats, censure, gazing at and touching women, / injury to others, and slander, he should carefully avoid.
A water pot, flowers, cow dung, clay, and kuśa grass / he should fetch as needed for food, and he should go begging for alms day by day.
Ghee, salt, and whatever is stale must all be avoided; / he should never watch dances, and must be free from desire for singing and the like.

He should not gaze at the sun, nor clean his teeth [with twigs];
[he should avoid] being alone while impure, and conversing with women, Śūdras, and the like.

He should consume the guru's leftovers or medicinal food, but not out of desire;
he should never perform a bath to scrub off dirt.

A brāhmaṇa should never set his mind on abandoning his guru;
if he abandons him out of delusion or greed, he becomes fallen.

From whomsoever he receives knowledge—whether worldly, Vedic,
or spiritual—he must never show hostility to him.

Manu has declared that one may abandon even a guru
who is arrogant, ignorant of what should and should not be done, and set upon a wrong path.

When the guru's own guru is present, he should behave toward him as toward his guru;
and when dismissed by his guru, he may salute his own elders.

This same constant conduct applies toward teachers of knowledge, toward ascetics,
toward those who restrain from unrighteousness, and those who teach what is beneficial.

Toward the guru's sons, his wives, and the guru's own relatives,
he should always maintain conduct as toward his own guru, for his own welfare.

A youth should honor those worthy of respect, or a trained pupil in ritual matters;
when teaching the guru's son, he deserves respect like a guru.

Rubbing of the limbs, bathing, eating his leftovers,
and washing the feet should not be done for the guru's son.

The guru's wives of equal caste are to be honored like the guru;
those of different castes are to be honored by rising up and saluting.

Anointing, bathing, massaging of the limbs,
and arranging of the hair should not be done for the guru's wife.

A young wife of the guru should not be saluted by touching her feet;
he should offer homage on the ground, saying, 'I am so-and-so.'

Returning from a journey, he should salute the guru's wives
by touching their feet, remembering the duty of the virtuous.

A maternal aunt, a maternal uncle's wife, a mother-in-law, and a paternal aunt
are to be honored like the guru's wife; they are equal to the guru's wife.

Sisters-in-law of equal caste should also be greeted every day;
and returning from a journey, the women related by blood and marriage should be greeted.

Toward a father's sister, a mother's sister, and an elder sister,
he should conduct himself as toward his mother; the mother is greater than they.

To [a student] endowed with such conduct, self-controlled, and free from deceit,
he should teach the Veda, righteousness, the Purāṇas, and the [Vedic] limbs constantly.

When a student has dwelt [with him] for a year, if the guru does not impart knowledge,
the guru takes upon himself the wrongdoing of that student residing with him.

A teacher's son, one eager to serve, one who imparts knowledge, one who is righteous, one who is pure,
one who is capable, one who gives food, one who gives water, and a good person: ten are to be taught according to dharma.

One who has memorized, one free from malice, an intelligent man, one who serves the guru,
one trustworthy, and one dear: these six twice-born men are to be taught according to rule.

To these brāhmaṇas, gifts [of learning] are given, but elsewhere according to what is fitting.
Having sipped water and restrained himself, he should always study facing north.

Grasping both his feet and looking at the guru's face,
he should say, 'Recite, sir!' and should stop when told, 'Let there be a pause.'

He should sit facing eastward grass, purified with blades of kuśa;
purified by three breath-controls, he is then worthy of the syllable Oṃ.

A brāhmaṇa should utter the Praṇava at the beginning and the end according to rule, O twice-born ones;
he should always perform teaching preceded by the clasping of hands for the Veda.

The Veda is the eternal eye of all beings;
he should study this constantly; otherwise he falls from brāhmaṇahood.

If he constantly studies the verses of the Ṛgveda, with an offering of milk he pleases the deities,
satisfying for a long time the gods invoked with desired objects.

Constantly studying the formulas of the Yajurveda, he pleases the deities with curd;
studying the melodies of the Sāmaveda, he pleases them daily with oblations of clarified butter.

Constantly studying the Atharvāṅgiras formulas, he pleases the deities with honey;
with the limbs of dharma and the Purāṇas, he satisfies the gods with meat offerings.

In the morning and in the evening, purified and observing the daily rule,
he should go to the forest and, collected in mind, recite the Gāyatrī.

A thousand times is the highest for the goddess, a hundred is middling, ten is lowest;
he should constantly mutter the Gāyatrī: this is proclaimed as the sacrifice of silent recitation.

The Lord weighed the Gāyatrī and the Vedas on a balance:
on one side the four Vedas, and on the other side the Gāyatrī.

Placing the syllable Oṃ at the beginning, then the sacred utterances immediately after,
he should thereafter recite the Sāvitrī, single-minded and endowed with faith.

Produced in a former cosmic age, eternal are 'Bhūḥ', 'Bhuvaḥ', and 'Svaḥ'—
these three great sacred utterances, destroyers of all inauspiciousness.

The primary material cause, the conscious soul, and time; Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara;
sattva, rajas, and tamas are traditionally remembered as the three sacred utterances in order.

The syllable [Oṃ] is the supreme Brahman; the Sāvitrī is next after that;
this mantra is the great yoga, proclaimed as the essence of the essence.

He who studies day after day this Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas,
understanding its meaning, as a celibate student, attains the supreme state.

The Gāyatrī is the mother of the Veda; the Gāyatrī is the purifier of the worlds;
there is no prayer higher than the Gāyatrī; knowing this, one is liberated.

On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O best of twice-borns,
or on that of Āṣāḍha or of Prauṣṭhapada, the commencement of Vedic study is prescribed.

During the southern course of the sun, for four and a half months,
a celibate student, concentrated in mind, should study in a clean place.

In the month of Pauṣa, a twice-born should perform outside the suspension of Vedic meters,
or on the arrival of the first day of the bright fortnight, in the forenoon.

A twice-born should practice the Vedic meters during the bright fortnight;
a man should study the Vedic limbs and the Purāṇas during the dark fortnights.

A student should always avoid these times unsuitable for study,
both when teaching and when practicing with effort:

When wind can be heard with the ear, at night; by day when dust is swirled up;
during lightning, thunder, and rain; and when large meteors fall;

Prajāpati declared that study is suspended on these occasions for an indeterminate time;
one should know these days as unsuitable for study when the sacrificial fires have been produced.

Then one should know that study is suspended when clouds appear out of season,
at a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the heavenly luminaries.

One should know these as occasions for indefinite suspension of study, even in season;
and when the fires have been kindled, at the sound of lightning and thunder.

During twilight study is suspended, as also during the remainder of the night as by day;
there is constant suspension of study in villages and in cities,

for those who desire proficiency in dharma, and always when there is a foul smell;
when a corpse is inside a village, and in the presence of a Śūdra;

suspension of study occurs when weeping is heard, and at the time of a downpour;
in water, at midnight, and while discharging feces and urine;

when impure with food remnants, and having eaten at an ancestral rite, he should not even think [of the Veda] in his mind;
when a learned twice-born receives the fee for a single-ancestor rite,

he should not cause the Veda to be recited for three days; and during birth or death impurity regarding the king or Rāhu,
as long as the food of one [family] remains in him, and as long as the grease does not disappear,

in the body of a learned brāhmaṇa, so long he should not recite the Veda;
lying down, sitting with raised knees, or sitting with a cloth bound around the legs,

he should not study; having eaten meat or the food of a Śūdra's ancestral rite;
in fog, at the sound of an arrow, and at both twilights;

on the new moon day, the fourteenth, the full moon, and the eighth days;
at the beginning of study and at the suspension of study, a fast of three nights is prescribed.
On the Aṣṭakās [study is suspended] for a whole day and night, and during the nights at the ends of seasons; / likewise in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, in Pauṣa, and likewise in Māgha.
Three Aṣṭakās during the dark fortnights have been declared by the wise. / In the shade of a śleṣmātaka tree, a śālmali tree, and a madhuka tree,
and under kovidāra and kapittha trees, one must never study. / When a fellow student has died, and likewise when a fellow celibate student has died,
and when the teacher has passed away, a three-night cessation of study is recorded. / These are the vulnerabilities of the brahmins, proclaimed as non-study periods.
Rākṣasas injure them during these times; therefore one should avoid them. / There is no non-study period for the daily obligatory rite and twilight devotion,
at the Upākarma, at the end of the fire offering, and likewise in the midst of the fire offering, / or for reciting a single Ṛg verse, a single Yajus formula, or Sāmans.

One should not study on the Aṣṭakās and similar occasions when a strong wind blows. / But there is no non-study suspension for the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, nor for legendary history and the Purāṇas,
nor for the legal treatises; one should avoid all these [non-study occasions for the Veda]. / This duty of the celibate student has been proclaimed in brief,
as formerly declared by Brahmā to the sages of cultivated minds. / The twice-born man who makes an effort elsewhere without having studied the Śruti,
is bewildered, excluded from the Veda, and should not be spoken to by twice-born men. / Nor should a twice-born man be content merely with the recitation of the Veda;
one whose limit is mere recitation sinks down like a cow in mud. / He who has studied the Veda according to rule, but does not reflect upon the meaning of the Veda,
is bewildered, like a Śūdra, and does not attain worthy recipient status. / If, however, he desires to dwell permanently with the guru,
he should serve him with restraint until the release of the body; / or having gone to the forest according to rule, he should offer oblations into the sacred fire,
and study daily, devoted to Brahman and concentrated; / he should constantly practice the Sāvitrī, the Śatarudrīya, and especially the Upaniṣads, / restrained and devoted to living on begged food.
This supreme, ancient rule of the Vedic tradition has been properly spoken to you here, / which the divine Manu Svāyambhuva declared of old when questioned by the foremost great sages.

3.54.m: Vyāsa said: / Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas and the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, O twice-born ones, / and having understood their meaning, the best of the twice-born should then take the ceremonial bath.
Having given wealth to the guru, he should take the bath with his permission. / Having crossed the vow, self-controlled and capable, he is fit to bathe.
He should carry a bamboo staff, an undergarment and an upper garment, / a pair of sacred threads, and a water-pot with water,
an umbrella, an immaculate turban, shoes and sandals, / and two golden earrings should be worn, with hair and nails clipped, pure.
Except for gold, the brahmin should not wear a red garland. / He should constantly wear white garments, be fragrant, and pleasant to behold.
He should not wear worn-out or dirty garments if he possesses wealth, / nor garments that are red or gaudy, nor clothes or earrings worn by another,
nor should he use the sandals, garland, or shoes of another, / displaying the sacred thread and ornament, or the black antelope skin.
He should not put on his garment to the right side, nor wear deformed clothing. / He should take a suitable and auspicious wife according to rule,
endowed with beauty and auspicious bodily marks, free from faults of birth, / not born from his father's lineage, but born of the lineage of another mortal,
a brahmin should take a wife endowed with good character and purity. / He should approach her during her fertile period until a son is born.
He should carefully avoid forbidden days: / the sixth, eighth, fifteenth, twelfth, and fourteenth lunar days;
he should remain celibate constantly on those, and likewise on the day of his three birth asterisms. / He should establish the nuptial fire and offer oblations into the sacred fire.
The initiated graduate should constantly purify these purifying rites. / He should unweariedly perform every day his own duty prescribed by the Veda.
Failing to do so, he quickly falls into most dreadful hells. / Restrained, he should practice the Veda and never neglect the great sacrifices.
He should perform household duties and twilight devotion; / he should cultivate friendship with his equals and superiors, and always approach the Lord.
He should visit the deities and provide nourishment for his wife. / The wise man should not broadcast his righteousness, nor should he conceal his sin.
He should constantly do what is good for himself, compassionate toward all living beings. / In conformity with his age, occupation, wealth, sacred learning, and lineage,
he should always conduct himself, acting in accordance with the region, speech, and intellect. / That conduct prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, properly practiced by the virtuous,
that custom he should observe; he should never strive for anything else. / By the path whereon his fathers have gone, and whereon his grandfathers have gone,
by that path of the virtuous he should go; going by it, he incurs no fault. / He should constantly be dedicated to Vedic recitation and always wear the sacred thread.
Truthful in speech, with anger conquered, free from greed and delusion, / devoted to muttering the Sāvitrī, performing ancestral rites, the householder is liberated.
Engaged in the welfare of his mother and father, devoted to the welfare of the brahmin, / generous, sacrificing, devoted to the gods, he is honored in the world of Brahmā.
Always pursuing the three aims of life, he should worship the gods / daily, day after day, and restrained, bow down to the gods.
Given constantly to sharing, endowed with patience, and compassionate: / he is truly called a householder; one is not a householder merely by possessing a house.
Patience, compassion, practical discernment, truth, self-restraint, tranquility, / constant devotion to the inner self, and knowledge: this is the mark of a brahmin.
The best of the twice-born should especially not neglect this. / Practicing righteousness to the best of his ability, he should avoid blameworthy deeds.
Shaking off the taint of delusion and attaining unsurpassed yoga, / the householder is freed from bondage; herein no doubt should be entertained.
Patience is the enduring of faults arising from mutual anger, / consisting of censured defeat, insult, violence, imprisonment, and murder of oneself.
Sympathy toward one's own sorrows, and benevolence toward the sorrows of others— / this the sages have called compassion, the direct means to righteousness.
Retaining the fourteen disciplines of learning for the sake of the supreme purpose: / that one should know as practical discernment, by which righteousness increases.
Having studied the learning according to rule and having understood its meaning, / one should perform righteous deeds; this indeed is called practical discernment.
By truth one conquers the world; truth is that supreme state. / The wise declare truth to be absence of error regarding reality as it is.
Self-restraint is the cessation of bodily actions; tranquility arises from clarity of intellect; / one should know the inner self as the imperishable, having gone whereto one does not grieve.
That knowledge by which that supreme, divine Blessed Lord, / Hṛṣīkeśa in person, is known, is proclaimed as knowledge.
Devoted to that, intent on that, wise, constantly free from anger, pure, / devoted to the great sacrifices, the brahmin attains that unsurpassed state.
One should diligently protect the body, which is the dwelling place of righteousness; / for without the body, the supreme Viṣṇu cannot be known by men.
Controlled, the twice-born should constantly apply himself to righteousness, wealth, and pleasure; / he should not even contemplate in his mind desire or wealth devoid of righteousness.
Even while perishing through righteousness, he should never practice unrighteousness; / for righteousness is the Blessed Lord, the refuge for all living creatures.
He should do what is agreeable to creatures, and his mind should not act to harm others; / he should not revile the Veda or the deities, nor should he associate with those who do.
But whatever restrained, pure mortal reads this chapter on dharma, / or teaches it or has it heard, is exalted in the world of Brahmā.
